To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the observed variability of gamma-ray bursts can be explained if the energy density of magnetic field is greater than about 0.01 times the energy density of thermal energy, and if the electrons are in equipartition (or nearly so) with the protons.

the observed rapid variability in the light curves of gamma-ray bursts requires that the magnetic field energy density in the radiating regions be greater than about one percent of the thermal energy and that the electrons be nearly in equiparition with the protones.

the observed temporal structure of GRB light curves is produced by the synchroton emission from electrons with Lorentz factors of about 100, and that the magnetic field in GRB sources has a strength of about 1 Gauss.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temporal structure of GRBs, which is a key to understanding the physics of these events.

a detailed analysis of gamma-ray bursts (and their afterglow) in the context of the fireball model and the implications of the model for the physics of the GRB emission region and the properties of the progenitor.
the temporal structure of gamma-ray bursts, the cooling time of the shocked plasma, the magnetic field strength in the fireball, and the radiation mechanisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the synchrotronic model for GRB emission is consistent with all observations, except for the break energy in the spectra, but is not inconsistent with any observation.
the observed temporal structure of GRBs is a consequence of the synchroton cooling of relativistic electrons in the forward and/or reverse shocks.
the synchroton model is consistent with the observational data, but it does not provide a complete explanation of all the observed properties of GRBs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fireball model is a promising model to explain the basic properties of the observed GRBs.
the observed variability of GRB light curves is most likely produced by synchrotron radiation in a magnetized, relativistic, thermal fireball.
the observed temporal and spectral properties of GRBs are consistent with a synchrotron origin, but the details are not well understood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the synchroton cooling time in GRBs is comparable to the variability time.
the temporal and spectral structure of GRBs is determined by the properties of the shocked material and not by the details of the emission mechanism.
a simple synchrotron model can account for the observed properties of GRB light curves and spectra, and that the observed properties are consistent with each other.
